content: Lithium-ion polymer batteries, commonly referred to as lithium polymer batteries or Li-poly (abbreviated as Li-Poly, Li-Pol, LiPo, LIP, or PLI), are rechargeable batteries that represent an evolution of lithium-ion battery technology. Unlike traditional lithium-ion batteries, where the lithium-salt electrolyte is dissolved in an organic solvent, lithium polymer batteries use a solid polymer composite, such as polyethylene oxide or polyacrylonitrile, to hold the electrolyte. The advantages of lithium polymer batteries over traditional lithium-ion designs include lower manufacturing costs and greater resistance to physical damage. These batteries first appeared in consumer electronics around 1996. Modern lithium polymer cells differ significantly from older lithium-ion cells. Traditional lithium-ion cells, whether cylindrical or prismatic, are encased in rigid metal housings. In contrast, lithium polymer cells use a flexible, foil-type polymer laminate casing, although they still contain organic solvents. The primary distinction lies in the structural design: lithium-ion cells rely on the rigid casing to press the electrodes and separator together, whereas lithium polymer cells achieve this through lamination of the electrode and separator sheets, eliminating the need for external pressure. The absence of a metal casing allows lithium polymer batteries to be lighter and more adaptable in shape, enabling them to be customized to fit specific devices. Additionally, the lack of intercell spacing and metal casing results in a higher energy density—over 20% greater than that of traditional lithium-ion batteries. They also store more energy than nickel-cadmium (NiCd) and nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries of the same volume. However, overcharging a lithium polymer battery can lead to catastrophic failure, including explosion or fire. Similarly, discharging a cell below 0 volts can render it incapable of holding a full charge or maintaining voltage under load. Early lithium polymer technology faced challenges such as high internal resistance, longer charging times, and slower maximum discharge rates compared to more mature battery technologies. Typically, these batteries require over an hour for a full charge. Recent advancements have improved discharge rates significantly, with some designs achieving discharge currents up to 15 or even 30 times the cell capacity. In 2005, Toshiba announced a new lithium polymer battery design capable of charging in just 1–3 minutes, though these cells have yet to reach the market. Such advancements are expected to have a transformative impact on industries like power tools, electric vehicles, and consumer electronics. Compared to lithium-ion batteries, lithium polymer batteries exhibit a higher rate of life cycle degradation. However, manufacturers now claim that these batteries can endure over 500 charge-discharge cycles before their capacity drops to 80%. A variant of lithium polymer cells, known as thin film rechargeable lithium batteries, has demonstrated the ability to provide more than 10,000 cycles. One of the most compelling advantages of lithium polymer cells is their design flexibility, allowing manufacturers to shape the batteries to fit specific applications. This is particularly valuable for mobile phone manufacturers striving to create smaller, thinner, and lighter devices. Additionally, lithium polymer cells have a much lower self-discharge rate compared to nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride cells. Lithium polymer batteries are increasingly popular in applications such as radio-controlled aircraft, where their lightweight and extended run times justify their cost. However, they require specialized chargers to prevent fire and explosion risks. Short-circuiting these batteries can also lead to explosions due to the rapid current flow through the cell. Enthusiasts in the radio-controlled community take precautions to ensure proper connection and insulation of battery leads. Specialized electronic motor speed controls are used to prevent excessive discharge, which could damage the battery. These controls typically include a low voltage cutoff (LVC) setting to maintain cell voltage at around 3 volts per cell. Lithium polymer batteries are also gaining traction in personal digital assistants (PDAs), laptops, and small digital music devices like iPods and MP3 players. They are desirable in applications where small form factors and high energy density outweigh cost considerations. These batteries are also being explored for use in next-generation electric vehicles, though the high cost of such vehicles remains a barrier. Proponents argue that increased production will drive down the cost of lithium polymer batteries. In terms of technology, there are currently two commercialized lithium-ion polymer battery designs, collectively referred to as polymer electrolyte batteries. These designs replace the traditional combination of a microporous separator and liquid electrolyte with an ion-conducting polymer. This approach offers improved safety, as polymer electrolytes are less prone to ignition, and enables the production of very thin battery cells without the need for external pressure to hold the electrodes together. The polymer electrolyte acts as a sealant, binding the electrodes together like glue. Some manufacturers, such as Avestor (now part of Batscap), use metallic lithium as the anode in lithium-metal-polymer batteries, while others prefer the safer carbon intercalation anode. Both commercialized technologies use a polymer (PVdF) gelled with conventional solvents and salts, such as EC/DMC/DEC. The main difference between the two technologies lies in the cathode material: one uses lithium manganese oxide (LiMn2O4), while the other employs the more conventional lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO2). More exotic lithium polymer batteries, not yet commercially available, use polymer cathodes. For example, Moltech is developing a battery with a plastic conducting carbon-sulfur cathode, though this technology has faced challenges with self-discharge and manufacturing costs. Another proposal involves using organic sulfur-containing compounds for the cathode in combination with an electrically conducting polymer like polyaniline. These designs promise low internal resistance and high discharge capacity but face issues with cycle life and cost. To prolong the life of lithium polymer batteries in multi-cell configurations, cell balancing is essential. Cell mismatches, whether in state-of-charge (SOC) or capacity/energy (C/E), can limit the overall battery pack capacity to that of the weakest cell. SOC mismatches are more common and can be addressed by balancing the cells during initial conditioning and subsequent charge phases. C/E mismatches are more challenging to address and require balancing during both charge and discharge cycles. Cell balancing involves applying differential currents to individual cells in a series string. Normally, all cells in a series string receive identical currents. A battery pack requires additional components and circuitry to achieve cell balancing. However, fully integrated analog front ends for cell balancing reduce the need for external components, requiring only balancing resistors. This approach eliminates the need for discrete capacitors, diodes, and most other resistors. A battery pack is considered balanced when all cells meet one of two conditions: (1) if all cells have the same capacity, they are balanced when they have the same relative SOC, as indicated by their open circuit voltage (OCV); or (2) if cells have different capacities, they are balanced when their SOC is the same, even though their absolute capacities differ. Maintaining balance in cells with different capacities requires differential current application during every charge and discharge cycle.
